colordle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Today's Colordle answer at a glance

The board settles on greyblue, rendered at hex #77A1B5. That's the official answer for day 1567, July 9, 2026. If you're looking at the clue card right now and seeing a muted blue-grey somewhere between slate and seafoam, you're already pointed in the right direction.

What kind of color this is

Greyblue lives in the cyan family, but it earns that placement loosely. The hex code breaks down to roughly 47% red, 63% green, and 71% blue—the green channel running notably higher than red gives it that cool, washed-out quality rather than true primary blue. Saturation sits around 30-35%, which means it lacks punch. Lightness hovers near the middle of the scale, so it's neither washed out nor deep.

Players who treat cyan-family colors as automatically teal will drift too far green. The correct path recognizes that greyblue sacrifices chroma for neutrality. It looks grey until you hold it next to something warmer, then the blue reveals itself. That's the core identity here—not bold, not pale, sitting in the uncomfortable middle where many solvers get stuck.

How to narrow your guesses toward it

Start by eliminating saturated blues and true greys. If you've placed any guesses with high saturation values (anything above 50% in the color picker), those aren't going to produce strong matches. Greyblue rewards low-to-mid saturation entries.

The recent history tells a useful story. Three days back, Cadet (#536872) showed up—that's a darker, more desaturated blue-grey. The proximity matters: if you played Cadet during its window and got partial information, you know approximately where greyblue lives on the lightness spectrum. The difference is that greyblue runs slightly lighter and carries marginally more blue saturation than Cadet did.

Working from the warm side also helps. Greys with yellow or pink undertones will register as misses, which immediately tells you the answer skews cool. From there, it's a matter of dialing in the exact saturation level—too low and you're guessing grey, too high and you're chasing sky blue.

Where players usually go wrong

The most common error with greyblue is assuming the "blue" descriptor means closer to cobalt or navy than it actually does. Players see the word and reach for saturated blues, burning guesses on colors that have no structural relationship to #77A1B5.

Another trap: treating cyan-family answers as interchangeable with teal. Teal pulls heavily green; greyblue keeps its green channel suppressed relative to blue. A guess that's visibly teal will show weak correlation even if the game technically classifies both as cyan-adjacent.

Some solvers also get caught overthinking the "grey" component. True greys—all three channels equalized—will miss completely. The answer has visible color. The grey qualifier describes restraint, not absence.

How the score logic actually helps

The scoring system flags partial matches based on how each RGB channel aligns with the target. For greyblue, you'll want to watch the blue channel specifically—if your guess undershoots the blue value significantly, that's a clear signal to push bluer. The green channel needs to stay controlled, not dominant.

When the system returns a low match score, resist the urge to jump to dramatically different hues. Greyblue rewards incremental adjustment. Move one channel at a time, observe the feedback, and let the board guide you back toward center rather than swinging to opposite corners of the color wheel.

The pattern becomes clearer after two or three educated guesses: if your blue channel response improves as you increase blue values, you're narrowing in. If adding blue makes the match worse, the answer probably runs cooler or less saturated than your current guess.

Questions players keep asking

Is greyblue closer to blue or grey?

Structurally, it's closer to blue—but only barely. The saturation is low enough that untrained eyes read it as grey. The distinction matters for gameplay: treat it as a desaturated blue with grey character, not a grey with blue hints.

Why does the game classify this as cyan instead of blue?

Cyan encompasses the range between blue and green. Greyblue falls into that band because its blue channel exceeds its red channel substantially while keeping the green channel lower than you'd find in true teal. The classification reflects the underlying RGB balance, not the everyday name you'd use at the paint store.

Without access to aggregate solve data, the honest answer is that it depends on starting position. Colors in the muted mid-range tend to fall within the third or fourth guess for players who've built good intuition for saturation differentials. First-time encounters may run longer.

It can work, but pure grey won't give you much signal since greyblue isn't grey. You're better off starting with a known blue variant slightly below mid-saturation. That guess tests both the hue family and the saturation range in a single move.

Colorfle answer today: how the mix should be read

The reveal card shows a target color sitting above three input slots. Each slot represents an RGB channel contribution. In additive mixing, red plus green makes yellow, green plus blue makes cyan, and red plus blue makes magenta. When all three overlap, you get white. A careful player reads the target as a combination problem, not a guessing game. If the target skews warm (orange-red tones), the puzzle wants more red channel contribution. Cool targets (blue-green) signal stronger blue and green inputs.

Most players who stumble on this puzzle do so because they mentally blend colors like paint. Pigment mixing follows subtractive rules—cyan absorbs red, magenta absorbs green, yellow absorbs blue. Colorfle operates on the opposite principle. More light added means brighter results. That's why the hint widgets on this page show intensity values rather than pigment ratios.

What the source colors are telling you

Each clue widget on today's page breaks the target into channel strength. Look for the R-G-B percentages listed under the hint section. These aren't arbitrary numbers—they map directly to how much each source color contributes to the final mix. A target showing 80% red intensity tells you to prioritize sources heavy in the red channel.

The archive link provides historical patterns worth studying. Players who track past solutions notice certain color families recur with predictable frequency. Warm neutrals appear roughly 40% of the time across the archive. Saturated primaries cluster in the remaining puzzles. Knowing this distribution helps narrow guesses before diving into detailed channel analysis.

The solver tool on this page accepts RGB hex values and returns a similarity score against the target. Run your best guess through the solver early. Even an approximate match reveals which channels need adjustment. If the solver shows 70% match but misses on blue, swap one source for something with stronger blue channel presence.

Why additive color logic beats random mixing

Random mixing wastes guesses. A systematic approach using channel math solves most Colorfle puzzles in two or three attempts. Here's the logic: treat the target as a vector in RGB space. Each source color is also a vector. The puzzle asks you to find three vectors that sum to or closely approximate the target vector.

This isn't abstract theory—it translates directly to solve strategy. Calculate what channel strengths the target needs. Select sources matching those strengths. Test with the solver. Adjust whichever channel falls short. Repeat until the match score hits acceptable range.

The clue widgets support this workflow by showing delta values between your current guess and the target. Those deltas tell you exactly which direction to shift each channel. Down on red? Replace a low-red source with something pulling harder into positive red territory. That kind of targeted revision beats cycling through unrelated colors every round.

Easy adjustment path for the next Colorfle

Before tomorrow's puzzle drops, establish a quick-reference mental model. Memorize the six secondary and tertiary colors formed from primary combinations: yellow (R+G), cyan (G+B), magenta (R+B), plus the intermediates like orange (heavy R, some G) and teal (heavy B, some G). When you see the target, identify its dominant channel(s) immediately.

Keep the solver bookmarked. Running guesses takes seconds and returns actionable feedback. Players who use the solver consistently solve faster than those relying on visual estimation alone. The numerical match score removes ambiguity that eyes can miss, especially with similar hues.

No. The puzzle sums all three inputs regardless of sequence. What matters is the combined channel contribution matching the target. Slot position has no effect on the final mix result.

The puzzle accepts matches above 85% similarity. Going higher improves your placement ranking, but anything clearing that bar counts as a solved puzzle. The solver displays exact percentage—aim for 90%+ if optimization matters to you.

How do I handle neutral gray targets?

Gray requires balanced RGB contributions. Select sources that collectively push all three channels toward equal mid-range values. Avoid heavily saturated inputs when targeting grays—the channel imbalance will show in the result.

Are there colors that never appear as targets?

Extremely saturated pure primaries rarely show up as final targets because the puzzle expects three-way combinations. You might see vivid red, but only if the other two sources contribute minimal green and blue. Check the archive to confirm which extremes actually occur versus which remain theoretical.

Contexto answer today: what the rank pattern usually means

A rank of 50 or lower typically signals you're in the right neighborhood—related concepts, adjacent ideas, or common co-occurrences. Most players start with direct synonyms and stall out around rank 100-300. The algorithm measures associative distance, not lexical overlap. If "sad" lands at rank 180, trying "unhappy" or "melancholy" wastes moves on lateral shifts within the same mental bucket.

Pivot instead. Jump to a different angle: causes of sadness, expressions of it, places where you'd find it, or objects associated with low mood. These category leaps often cut ranks by half in a single guess because they explore fresh semantic territory the algorithm hasn't already scored nearby.

The solver link in the sidebar lets you test category hypotheses before committing guesses. Use it to probe whether "weather" relates to your target through location, mood, or event—that distinction determines your next move.

Why broad words beat clever words here

Specific, artistic, or unusual vocabulary tends to score poorly in Contexto. The system maps common usage patterns, not rare coinages. "Melancholia" sits further from most targets than "sadness" despite being semantically equivalent. Broad, everyday terms cluster near the center of the association map; niche words scatter toward the edges.

This means "car" outperforms "sedan," "beach" beats "seaside resort," and "food" trumps "cuisine" in most contexts. Save the precision for when you've narrowed the field and need to distinguish between tight candidates. Early guesses should be blunt instruments, not surgical tools.

Archive data from past puzzles shows that successful runs share one habit: they front-load breadth. Players who exhaust direct synonyms first typically need 15-20 attempts. Those who jump between categories early finish in 8-12.

Tonight's archive entry logs the full sequence once you solve or abandon the puzzle. Reviewing that history trains pattern recognition for future boards. Pay attention to which categories the solution fell into—that shapes how you'll open tomorrow.

No. Each guess receives an independent similarity score based on its relationship to the target. Previous guesses don't influence the ranking—only the hidden word matters.

Contexto measures associative distance, not logical closeness. An obvious guess shares a category with the target, while a random-feeling word might accidentally sit closer on the association graph. This gap reveals why category pivots matter more than synonym refinement.

How generation, type, and stage narrow the pool

Which guesses pull double duty best

How to finish the next Quordle with fewer panicked guesses

Should I focus on one board at a time or all four together?

All four together, especially in early and mid-game. Early focus on one board means wasting guesses that could have narrowed options on the others. Mid-game, when boards diverge significantly, it's fine to switch to single-board mode for the hardest remaining puzzles.

How autocomplete logic narrows the answer

Google's autocomplete draws from real query data, which means it favors recency, regional popularity, and cultural momentum. A phrase that dominated searches three years ago might not appear in predictions today if interest has cooled. Conversely, a niche topic that went viral last month can suddenly dominate autocomplete results.

Why obvious phrasing usually wins

Most Searchle players overthink their guesses. They try to anticipate clever wordplay when the puzzle is really testing whether you understand how people actually search. Casual searchers don't optimize their language. They type what's natural, often incomplete, occasionally wrong.

Questions players keep asking

Does autocorrect affect Searchle predictions?

Google's autocomplete sometimes corrects misspellings in predictions, but not always. Regional variations and older query data can preserve typos that persist in popular searches. Testing your guess through the solver can reveal whether an alternate spelling ranks higher.

Semantle answer today: what the warm scores are pointing toward

If your recent guesses are scoring in the 30s, you're in the right neighborhood. A score of 30-50 puts you in the outer ring of warmth—the kind of zone where most players start adjusting their mental model of what the answer might be. How to explore a semantic lane on purpose

Rather than throwing unrelated words at the board, pick a direction and commit. If "ocean" scored 45, try other liquid or depth-related terms. "Tide," "current," "marine"—these live in the same conceptual neighborhood. Each guess refines your map of the answer's territory. The archive link on this page lets you compare how past puzzles behaved when players hit similar score ranges, which can sharpen your sense of how far a given lane extends before it goes cold.

When simple words do more than precise ones

Specificity sometimes backfires early. A guess like "photosynthesis" might score lower than expected because it's too narrow—you're betting everything on one exact concept. Broader terms like "process," "nature," or "growth" can score surprisingly well because they capture dimensions of the answer without pinning you to a single narrow definition. Save the precision for when you're in the 70+ range and need to differentiate between closely related candidates.

How to reset without wasting twenty guesses

Players who feel stuck often keep hammering away at the same semantic area, losing five or six guesses to diminishing returns. A better move: deliberately jump to an orthogonal concept. If you've been circling physical objects, try something abstract. If emotional terms haven't worked, shift to mathematical or scientific vocabulary. You lose maybe two guesses to the pivot, but you gain information about whether the answer lives in that direction at all. The solver tool on this page can help you identify which guess patterns tend to break through plateaus based on aggregate player data.

Questions players keep asking

What does the score actually measure?

The score reflects Word2vec cosine similarity—essentially how often your word appears in similar contexts to the secret word across a large text corpus. Two words with a score of 80 aren't necessarily synonyms; they're used in comparable ways by writers and speakers. That's why seemingly off-base guesses sometimes score higher than you'd expect.

Why did my good guess suddenly drop in score?

Scores can fluctuate slightly depending on how the embedding model weights context. More commonly, though, you've simply moved past the peak overlap point. A guess at 68 might represent the closest you've been—but if the next few guesses drift in the wrong direction, the score will reflect that descent. Think of it as climbing a hill: you might be near the top but not exactly there yet.

Mario characters alone eliminate roughly 80 fighters from the total roster, and if the board shows multiple universes represented, you're already narrowing the field more efficiently than any other single clue.

Smashdle answer today: which fighter clue matters first

Universe classification cuts deepest because it groups fighters by source game rather than mechanics. A Zelda universe answer eliminates every Fire Emblem, Pokemon, and third-party character instantly. Weight class comes second—it splits the remaining candidates into featherweight, middleweight, and heavyweight brackets that don't overlap. Jump count then layers on top of those two, creating a three-tier filter that typically leaves just 3-5 possibilities before you even touch damage stats or final smashes.

The mistake most players make is starting with final smash animations. Those are visually distinctive but slow to parse, and several fighters share similar-looking finishers. Universe and movement data get you to the answer faster when used in the right order.

How universe and movement stats split the roster

Smash Bros hosts fighters from roughly 15 distinct universes, plus a handful of third-party guests. Each universe has its own flavor—Retro games cluster heavy hitters, modern Nintendo franchises favor speed, and indie crossovers tend toward unique movement kits. On today's board, a careful player would notice how the archive section tracks past reveals, letting you spot patterns in which universe types appear most frequently across recent days.

Movement stats break down into five categories: run speed, walk speed, air speed, jump height, and fall speed. These numbers aren't arbitrary—they reflect how each fighter actually plays. A fast-faller with high air speed plays differently than a floaty with low jump count, and that distinction matters for elimination. If you've narrowed candidates to two fighters from the same universe, movement stats usually decide it.

Weight class interacts with these movement values in ways that matter. A super heavyweight can't outrun a projectile, but they can tank hits that would KO a featherweight. When both candidates share similar speeds, weight class becomes the tiebreaker.

Why DLC fighters cause so many misses

DLC fighters complicate the board because they're not in the base roster most players default to mentally. Sephiroth moves like no one else in the Final Fantasy lineup. Kazuya plays nothing like the other Smash reps. When a DLC fighter appears on today's board, universe might point correctly but movement stats catch players off guard because they've never internalized those values.

How to tighten the next Smashdle faster

Practice makes pattern recognition faster. After each solve, note which clue chain led you there—was it universe first, then weight, then jumps? Or did final smash animation clinch it when stats couldn't? Over time, you'll develop a personal hierarchy that matches your memory strengths.

The archive linked on this page lets you review past puzzles without spoiling today's answer. Use it to drill universe groupings when you notice gaps in your knowledge. Missing too many Zelda reps? Spend ten minutes with the roster list. Confusing which Pokemon are in the same evolution family? That matters for some puzzle variants.

For tomorrow's puzzle, try this approach: scan all available clues once before guessing. Mark the universe, weight class, and jump count mentally. Then cross-reference against your mental roster shortlist. Only when that fails should you dig into damage, final smash, or other granular details.

Does the order of clues on the board affect solve priority?

No. The layout varies daily, but the clues themselves stay consistent. Universe and movement stats remain the most reliable filters regardless of where they appear on screen.

Echo fighters share universe and weight class with their source fighter, but movement stats often diverge enough to distinguish them. Daisy versus Peach is a common confusion point—look at fall speed and air acceleration rather than raw jump height.

Spotle answer today: which clue should matter first

Genre narrows the field more aggressively than any other single category. If the reveal card shows "rock" versus "pop," you're immediately excluding 60-70% of possible artists from consideration. A duo suggests a specific collaborative history; a five-piece band implies certain structural decisions about sound. This clue often trips up players who assume the obvious genre match without checking whether the artist fits the scale.

The hint widget on today's page lets you reveal one category partially. Use it strategically—if you've narrowed to three possibilities based on genre and group size, the partial country or era reveal can cut two of those out instantly.

How genre, country, and era work together

These three clues form a triangle that most solvers underestimate. An artist from Nigeria in the 2010s working in Afrobeats follows a completely different release pattern than a UK artist in the same era working in grime. Artists who emerged before streaming changed how music gets distributed tend to have catalog sizes that influence their cultural footprint differently than post-2010 artists. Confirmation bias drives most incorrect answers. Players see an artist they recognize fitting three clues and force the fourth or fifth to match rather than accepting the mismatch means a different answer. If your guess has a different group size than what's revealed, start over—the category constraints are non-negotiable.

Gender clues trip up players who assume based on genre stereotypes. Some genres skew heavily male in public perception but have significant female representation. The clue exists precisely because it challenges assumptions. Take it literally.

Best way to solve the next Spotle faster

Build a mental database of artists sorted by their unusual combination traits. Most players think in individual artists; better solvers think in patterns. Which swaps usually unlock two words at once

Swapping two misaligned letters that sit at word intersections tends to resolve two directions simultaneously. When Letter A belongs in Position X and Letter B belongs in Position Y, swapping them fixes both spots if X and Y fall within crossing words.

Players who track swap efficiency notice that corner-adjacent pairs behave differently than center-adjacent pairs.
